seo.title: Kitchen Chimney Cost in India (2026): Buying Guide
seo.description: Kitchen chimney cost in India for 2026, plus how to choose: auto-clean vs baffle, suction power, size, ducting and how a chimney fits your modular kitchen.

title: Kitchen Chimney Buying Guide: Auto-Clean vs Manual, Cost & What Fits Your Modular Kitchen
author: Shivam Kumar

featuredImage.alt: Stainless steel pyramid chimney mounted above a glass cooktop in a modern kitchen

excerpt: Chimney prices run from ₹5,000 to over ₹1 lakh, and the cheapest and most expensive models both claim to suit your kitchen. See real cost bands, auto-clean vs baffle, suction needs and how to fit one into a modular kitchen.
keyTakeaways: Budget ₹12,000–₹18,000 for a Good Auto-Clean Chimney — Entry models start around ₹5,000; premium ₹20,000–₹35,000; designer and imported hoods go past ₹50,000.
Match Suction to Your Cooking, Not the Highest Number — 1,000–1,200 m³/hr for daily cooking, 1,200–1,500 m³/hr for heavy frying; a short straight duct matters as much as the rating.
Size the Chimney to the Hob — 60 cm for 2 burners, 75 cm for 3, 90 cm for 4–5; undersized chimneys miss smoke from outer burners.
Auto-Clean Is a Convenience Upgrade, Not a Necessity — Baffle filters cost less and never need replacing, just regular washing.
Plan the Duct Route Before the Hob Position — The hob should follow the duct, not the other way round, with as few bends as possible.
Ducted Beats Ductless for Indian Cooking — Ductless recirculating models struggle with heavy frying and tadka; use them only when a real duct isn't possible.
contentHtml:
A good kitchen chimney for an Indian home typically costs about ₹12,000 to ₹18,000 for an auto-clean model with adequate suction, and ₹20,000 to ₹35,000 for premium models; designer and imported hoods go well above ₹50,000. Choose 1,000 to 1,200 m³/hr suction for regular daily cooking and 1,200 to 1,500 m³/hr for heavy frying, match the width to your hob, mount it about 61 to 76 cm above the hob, and use a short, straight duct to the outside.

Indian cooking produces smoke, oil and strong smells, and a good chimney is what keeps them out of the rest of the house and off your cabinets. But chimney prices run from about ₹5,000 to over ₹1 lakh, and the cheapest model in the shop and the most expensive both claim to be right for your kitchen. This guide covers kitchen chimney cost in India, the difference between auto-clean and manual models, and how to choose one that fits your cooking and your modular kitchen.

Key facts at a glance

QuestionShort answer
What does a kitchen chimney cost?About ₹12,000 to ₹18,000 for a quality auto-clean model; ₹20,000 to ₹35,000 premium
Cheapest branded models?From about ₹5,000 to ₹6,000
Suction for daily Indian cooking?1,000 to 1,200 m³/hr; 1,200 to 1,500 m³/hr for heavy frying
What size?60 cm for 2-burner hobs, 75 cm for 3 burners, 90 cm for 4 to 5 burners
Height above the hob?About 24 to 30 inches (61 to 76 cm)
Duct size?6 inch (150 mm) for 60 cm models; 8 inch (200 mm) for 90 cm and larger
Installation charge?From about ₹500 for a wall-mounted unit, more for island and ceiling types

How much does a kitchen chimney cost in India?

Budget bandTypical priceWhat you get
Entry levelAbout ₹5,000 to ₹10,000Basic baffle-filter models, lower suction, push-button controls
Mid rangeAbout ₹12,000 to ₹18,000Auto-clean, 1,200+ m³/hr suction, touch or gesture controls
PremiumAbout ₹20,000 to ₹35,000Quieter motors, filterless designs, better finishes and controls
Designer and imported₹50,000 to over ₹1 lakhIsland and ceiling hoods, smart features, European brands

Published 2026 price ranges for major brands illustrate the spread: Hindware from about ₹4,800, Elica from about ₹6,000, Faber from about ₹6,300 and Bosch from about ₹14,300, with top models from several brands priced above ₹50,000. Prices change often with sales and new models, so treat these as a guide.

Remember the extras: installation, ducting, any civil work to make an outlet, and the electrical point.

Auto-clean vs manual (baffle) chimneys

FactorAuto-clean (filterless or heat-clean)Manual baffle filter
How it worksHeat melts collected oil, which drains into a removable oil collectorStainless steel baffles trap grease, which you clean by hand
UpkeepEmpty the oil collector; occasional wipe-downWash the baffle filters regularly
CostHigherLower
Suction over timeHolds steady with less effortDrops if filters are not cleaned
Best forDaily, heavy Indian cooking; busy householdsLighter cooking; tight budgets

Both types work for Indian cooking. Auto-clean is mainly a convenience upgrade: it reduces how often you clean, not whether you need to. Baffle filters never need replacing, only washing.

Ducted or ductless? Ducted chimneys push smoke outside and are recommended for Indian cooking. Ductless (recirculating) models filter and return air to the kitchen and work less well with heavy frying and tadka. Use ductless only where a duct to the outside is truly impossible.

How much suction do you need?

Cooking styleRecommended suction
Light cooking, 2 to 3 times a week800 to 1,000 m³/hr
Regular daily cooking1,000 to 1,200 m³/hr
Heavy daily frying, grilling and spices1,200 to 1,500 m³/hr

Higher suction is not always better. A very powerful chimney in a small closed kitchen is louder without being more effective. Suction also falls with every extra metre of duct and every bend, so a modest chimney with a short, straight duct often outperforms a powerful one with a long, twisting duct. Budget models typically run at 65 to 70 decibels; premium models at 50 to 55.

For semi-open and open kitchens, where smells drift into the dining area, size up. Our Dwarka Expressway kitchen layout guide suggests 1,200+ m³/hr for semi-open kitchens.

What size chimney fits your hob?

HobChimney width
2-burner60 cm
3-burner75 cm
4 or 5-burner90 cm

The chimney should be at least as wide as the hob, so it captures smoke from every burner. For heavy frying on a 4-burner hob, a 90 cm chimney works better than a 60 cm one.

Chimney types and where they fit

TypeWhere it fitsNotes
Wall-mountedHob against a wall, the most common setupWidest choice and simplest installation
Built-in or integratedHidden inside a wall cabinetClean look; check suction and access for cleaning
IslandHob on a kitchen islandNeeds a ceiling duct route; costlier to install
CeilingFlush with the false ceilingPremium look; needs ceiling depth and a duct route
CornerHob in a cornerLimited models

In most Gurgaon apartments, a wall-mounted or built-in chimney over a wall hob is the practical choice. Island hobs need a ceiling duct route, which many apartments cannot provide. Our kitchen layout guide explains why we usually keep the hob on the wall.

Fitting a chimney into a modular kitchen

Plan the chimney with the kitchen, not after it:

  1. Fix the duct route first. Find the external wall or shaft outlet before deciding where the hob goes. The hob follows the duct.
  2. Keep the duct short and straight. Use a 6 inch (150 mm) duct for 60 cm models and 8 inch (200 mm) for 90 cm and larger, with as few and as gentle bends as possible.
  3. Mount at the right height: about 24 to 30 inches (61 to 76 cm) above the hob, or 26 to 28 inches (66 to 71 cm) for high-flame, heavy-oil cooking.
  4. Leave clearance: about 2 to 3 inches from adjacent wall cabinets.
  5. Plan the power point: a 15-amp socket with proper earthing, hidden inside the chimney cover or an adjacent cabinet.
  6. Box the duct neatly: inside a wall cabinet or false-ceiling bulkhead, with an access panel for future service.
  7. Check society rules: some Gurgaon high-rises restrict new openings in external walls, so confirm before cutting.

For small kitchens, see our small modular kitchen design ideas.

Installation cost

Brand installation is usually inexpensive. One manufacturer's published charges, excluding taxes and civil work:

TypeIndicative installation charge
Wall-mountedAbout ₹500 to ₹650
Split chimneyAbout ₹1,500 to ₹1,750
Island chimneyAbout ₹1,750 to ₹2,500
Ceiling chimneyAbout ₹2,500 to ₹3,200

Civil work, such as cutting an outlet through a wall, extra ducting, boxing and a new electrical point, is extra and can cost more than the installation itself.

Maintenance

TaskHow often
Wipe the body and glassWeekly
Wash baffle filters (manual models)Every few weeks with heavy cooking
Run auto-clean and empty the oil collectorAs the manufacturer's indicator or manual advises
Check the duct for grease build-upYearly
Professional serviceAs required, or under the brand's service plan

Warranties on many models run long, but they cover the product, not the installation or ducting. Check the authorised service network in Gurgaon before you buy. For what an interior firm's warranty covers versus the brand's, see our interior design warranty guide.

Seven questions to ask before you buy

  1. Is my kitchen closed, semi-open or open?
  2. How heavy is my daily cooking?
  3. How many burners does my hob have?
  4. Where will the duct exit, and how long will it be?
  5. Auto-clean or baffle: how much cleaning will I actually do?
  6. How loud is it at the speed I will use most?
  7. Is there an authorised service centre near me?

faqs.question: What is the cost of a kitchen chimney in India?
faqs.answer: Kitchen chimneys cost from about ₹5,000 for entry-level models. A quality auto-clean chimney with adequate suction typically costs ₹12,000 to ₹18,000, premium models ₹20,000 to ₹35,000, and designer island and imported hoods ₹50,000 to over ₹1 lakh.

faqs.question: Which is better, an auto-clean or a baffle filter chimney?
faqs.answer: Both work for Indian cooking. Auto-clean chimneys melt and collect oil, so they need less frequent cleaning and hold suction better, but they cost more. Baffle filter chimneys are cheaper and the filters never need replacing, but they must be washed regularly.

faqs.question: How much suction does a kitchen chimney need for Indian cooking?
faqs.answer: About 1,000 to 1,200 m³/hr for regular daily cooking and 1,200 to 1,500 m³/hr for heavy frying and spices. Light cooking needs only 800 to 1,000 m³/hr. A short, straight duct matters as much as the suction rating.

faqs.question: What size chimney should I buy?
faqs.answer: Match the chimney to the hob: 60 cm for a 2-burner hob, 75 cm for 3 burners and 90 cm for 4 or 5 burners. For heavy frying on a 4-burner hob, choose 90 cm.

faqs.question: How high should a chimney be installed above the gas hob?
faqs.answer: About 24 to 30 inches (61 to 76 cm) above the hob, or 26 to 28 inches (66 to 71 cm) for high-flame, heavy-oil cooking. Always follow the specific model's installation manual.

faqs.question: Is a ducted or ductless chimney better?
faqs.answer: Ducted chimneys are better for Indian kitchens because they push smoke and grease outside. Ductless chimneys recirculate filtered air and work less well with heavy frying. Use ductless only if a duct to the outside is not possible.

faqs.question: How much does chimney installation cost?
faqs.answer: Brand installation for a wall-mounted chimney can start at about ₹500, with island and ceiling chimneys costing more. Civil work, extra ducting, boxing and a new electrical point are usually extra.
